scenario: A 62-year-old Japanese man was diagnosed with submandibular salivary duct carcinoma (T4bN3cM0 according to Union for International Cancer Control, 8th edition). He had alcohol use disorder with facial flushing after small amounts of alcohol, suggestive of aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) deficiency—a common genetic polymorphism in East Asian populations. He underwent right neck dissection with skin resection, reconstruction using a pectoralis major flap, and adjuvant radiotherapy (66 Gy). He remained free of recurrence on regular clinical and computed tomography (CT) surveillance but continued daily heavy alcohol consumption. Three years later, he developed progressive frailty with 3 months of reduced oral intake. Neurologic examination revealed diminished superficial sensation, dysesthesia, and impaired proprioception in the lower extremities, consistent with sensory ataxia in a polyneuropathy pattern. Laboratory testing at that time showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 9.1 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]; mean corpuscular volume, 101.4 μm3(to convert to femtoliters, multiply by 1), and vitamin B12supplementation was initiated. In this clinical context, his sensory-dominant polyneuropathy was suspected to be related to chronic alcohol use and vitamin B12/folate deficiency. Spinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), performed to evaluate for structural causes of neurologic symptoms, revealed multiple hypointense lesions on T1-weighted images in the thoracolumbar spine (Figure 1A); similar findings were observed on T2-weighted imaging (image not shown). The corresponding CT image demonstrated mild hyperdensity with ill-defined margins without cortical destruction (Figure 1B). Given his oncologic history and the imaging findings, a CT-guided biopsy of the signal alteration in the T12 vertebral body was performed by an orthopedic spine surgeon for definitive diagnosis.
